It belongs on this map as part of the industry rather than as a source about it: an association exists to make its members' case, and it does so competently, which is precisely why its figures circulate further than the regulators' own.

properties.name: SGS — agricultural field studies division
properties.desc: One of the largest testing and inspection companies on Earth runs supervised field trials as a contract service, and lists genetically modified biosafety alongside good laboratory and good experimental practice among the standards its network of research centres works to. The services offered include residue, efficacy, environmental fate, non-target organism and operator exposure studies. Those are the study types a regulator reads before deciding on a release, and they are commissioned and paid for by the applicant. The trial is run by neither the company seeking the permit nor the agency granting it, and the contractor's obligation runs to whoever holds the contract.

properties.name: Eurofins Agroscience Services
properties.desc: Assembled by buying up the agrochemical industry's established contract research laboratories and welding them into a single global offering, this arm of Eurofins conducts field and laboratory studies on new substances and new crop varieties and then also provides the regulatory service that compiles the resulting dossier. It states plainly that it supports plant breeders and the seed industry as well as pesticide manufacturers. Consolidation matters here more than size: when the independent laboratories that once checked each other are bought into one company, a second opinion becomes a second department.

properties.name: Eurofins Advinus
properties.desc: The Indian arm of the same group, running multi-location field trials across the country's climatic zones for manufacturers of agricultural inputs, with trial officers placed nationwide and data generated to standards intended for submissions elsewhere as well as at home. India is where a great deal of the world's field data is now produced for regulators who will never visit the plots. The country hosting the trial and the country reading the result are increasingly not the same country.

properties.name: Staphyt
properties.desc: A European agroscience contractor holding a network of officially recognised trial stations, with field agronomists and project managers who test both products and varieties for performance, efficacy and safety, and a regulatory affairs department that designs the studies. Its own description of the arrangement is the useful part: the two capabilities are combined so a client can be supported from early development through to launch. A study designed by the same firm that will argue it through a regulator is a different object from one designed to find out.

properties.name: Boehringer Ingelheim — RABORAL V-RG production
properties.state: Lyon — Boehringer Ingelheim Animal Health, 29 Avenue Tony Garnier
properties.desc: An engineered virus scattered across landscapes by aircraft, by the hundred million. RABORAL V-RG is an attenuated vaccinia virus carrying the rabies glycoprotein gene, packed in fishmeal-coated sachets and dropped into wildlife habitat for foxes, raccoons, coyotes and jackals to eat. It has been in continuous use since it was first field tested in foxes in Belgium in 1987, and roughly 250 million doses have been distributed worldwide since. It is one of two oral bait vaccines the World Health Organization recommends for wildlife rabies control, and its field use has been credited with eliminating wildlife rabies from Belgium, France and Luxembourg and the dog and coyote rabies variant from the United States. It is also the largest deliberate environmental release of an engineered organism anywhere on this map, and it is a public health programme rather than a commercial planting — which is exactly why it belongs here. The category of release is not defined by whether the purpose is good.

properties.name: USDA APHIS Wildlife Services
properties.desc: The manufacturer sells this vaccine only to government agencies running rabies control programmes; no private buyer can obtain it. Distribution is by state and federal wildlife services, and the public-facing instruction where baits land in gardens and streets is to leave them alone and telephone a control programme. That structure is worth noting precisely because it is unusual on this map: an engineered organism released into the open where the release is planned by a public agency, the product cannot be bought, and a member of the public who finds one is given a number to call. Most releases documented here have none of those three features.

properties.name: Demanda Colectiva en Defensa del Maíz Nativo
properties.state: Mexico City — Twelfth Federal District Court for Civil Matters
properties.desc: Fifty-three farmer, consumer and environmental organisations filed a collective action in July 2013 arguing that engineered maize threatened the native varieties of the crop's centre of origin, and that the constitution's guarantee of a healthy environment covered it. A precautionary measure issued that September halted every authorisation to plant engineered maize in Mexico. What makes this the most instructive case on the map is what happened next: the government and the companies brought roughly a hundred legal challenges, producing 22 amparo judgments resolved by 17 different federal courts and by the Supreme Court, and the measure survived all of them. In 2017 the Court's First Chamber declined even to docket Monsanto's appeal. A precautionary suspension that is cheap to obtain and expensive to overturn is a different instrument from a ban, and this is the worked example of it.

properties.name: Monsanto Co. v. Geertson Seed Farms
properties.state: Washington DC — Supreme Court of the United States
properties.desc: The first engineered-crop case the US Supreme Court decided, in June 2010. Conventional alfalfa growers had shown that the Agriculture Department deregulated Roundup Ready alfalfa without the environmental impact statement the law required, and a district court enjoined all planting until one was done. The Supreme Court reversed the injunction 7–1 while leaving the underlying finding untouched: an agency breach of environmental law does not by itself entitle anyone to an injunction. The half worth keeping is the standing holding — the growers had it, because the district court found a reasonable probability that their crops would carry the engineered gene, and that risk injured them by itself. Justice Stevens, dissenting, set out the findings the majority did not dispute: the crop can reach other plants, it had done so even under controlled planting, and the agency had limited ability to monitor or enforce the limits it set.

properties.name: Kenyan GMO petitions (consolidated)
properties.state: Nairobi — High Court of Kenya and the Environment and Land Court
properties.desc: Kenya lifted a ten-year ban on engineered organisms in 2022 and was immediately taken to court. The petitions raised freedom of conscience, the right of access to information, the right to food of acceptable quality, and whether the regulations in place were sufficient. The Environment and Land Court ruled in 2023 and the consolidated petitions were dismissed in 2024. The case belongs here for two reasons and neither is the outcome. It shows what a challenge to a lifting looks like as opposed to a challenge to an approval, and it shows the cost of pendency working the other way: four Bt cotton varieties recommended for release, and six more through national performance and distinctness testing, sat unreleased while it ran. A case that is lost can still have suspended a release for two years, and a case that is won can be undone by the same delay in reverse.

properties.name: SOFITEX — Société Burkinabè des Fibres Textiles
properties.desc: Burkina Faso began field trials in 2003 with Monsanto, which agreed to cross the Bt gene into local varieties; those went to farmers in 2008, and by 2014 the country had more engineered-crop growers than anywhere else in Africa, over 140,000 of them smallholders. Then the companies withdrew it. The Burkinabè cotton the Bt trait was crossed into came from a seventy-year breeding programme built for staple length and ginning ratio, and the engineered cultivars produced shorter lint and less of it — by 2013/14 more than two thirds of the national crop had dropped to the lower-quality medium staple class, with the ginning ratio below the 42 per cent the non-engineered cultivars reached. Cottonseed went from 53 per cent Bt in 2015/16 to a planned 30 per cent the following season and a full return to conventional seed for 2017/18, and the cotton companies asked Monsanto for compensation reported at around 280 million dollars. Note who bore the loss and who did not: farmers sold at a guaranteed price and were largely unaffected, so the failure registered only because it landed on the companies. A trait can raise yield and still destroy the value of the crop, and yield is what the trials measured.

properties.name: Agence Nationale de Biosécurité (Burkina Faso)
properties.desc: The national biosafety agency, which parliament converted from a departmental body into an administrative entity with its own legal authority and independent management. That change was made in the same period the country was withdrawing Bt cotton, and the sequence is the point: a regulator gains independence most readily just after the thing it was regulating has gone wrong. West Africa's biosafety decisions are made here and in Abuja more than anywhere else on the continent, and this agency is the one whose country has actually reversed a commercial approval.

properties.name: Parliament of Uganda
properties.desc: Parliament passed a national biosafety act on 4 October 2017. The president declined to sign it and returned it, asking for changes to the title, to the patent rights of indigenous farmers, and for sanctions where engineered material is mixed with indigenous crops and animals. The bill was rewritten and renamed the Genetic Engineering Regulatory Bill, passed again in November 2018, and refused assent a second time in 2019, this time over separation of engineered and non-engineered material and over labelling. His stated reason on liability is the substantive part: the burden of proof should sit with whoever introduced the material, because a peasant farmer cannot marshal the financial and administrative resources to assemble scientific and legal evidence in court. Uganda's constitution requires a two-thirds majority of all members to pass a bill the president has returned twice; the parliamentary term lapsed without that vote. So a country with an active crop biotechnology programme has run for years with no biosafety statute at all — which is a different condition from a ban, and a worse one for anyone trying to object to a particular release.

properties.name: Abitrigo
properties.state: São Paulo — Associação Brasileira da Indústria do Trigo
properties.desc: Brazil's flour milling association said its members would stop buying Argentine wheat altogether if Brazil approved engineered wheat imports, a position shared by the groups representing bakers and other wheat processors. Around 80 per cent of Brazil's wheat imports come from Argentina, so the threat was substantial. When the biosafety commission approved the flour anyway, the association asked the president's office to convene a national biosecurity committee to review the decision. This is the clearest example on the map of the veto that sits downstream of a regulator: an approval grants permission to sell and does not oblige anyone to buy, and a processing industry that refuses can hold a cleared product off the market more effectively than an objection filed during the comment window.

properties.name: Sinogene Biotechnology
properties.desc: A commercial pet-cloning company that also clones for the police. It sells copies of dead pets at around fifty thousand dollars, and separately produced Kunxun, China's first cloned police dog, from a Kunming wolfdog credited with helping solve twelve murder cases — work done with Yunnan Agricultural University and the support of the Ministry of Public Security. In November 2019 six cloned dogs were sworn into the Beijing police, their DNA more than 99 per cent identical to two Belgian Malinois chosen for their record on the force. The economic case is training rather than biology: conventional training runs about five years and up to half a million yuan with no guarantee of success. The company's own scientist concedes clones share appearance and general health but that upbringing may still make behaviour differ, and a veterinarian quoted alongside notes China has no animal protection law under which pet cloning could be regulated. The surrogate mothers that carry these pregnancies are the part of the service that has no customer.

properties.name: Boyalife–Sooam joint venture, Tianjin
properties.desc: A joint venture between a Chinese biotechnology firm, the Korean dog-cloning foundation and two Chinese research institutions, announced as the world's largest animal cloning facility: pet and police dogs, racehorses and beef cattle for the open market, starting at 100,000 cattle embryos a year and stated as growing towards a million. Whatever the plant has actually produced since, the announcement itself marks the transition this facet is about. Cloning stopped being a demonstration that a thing is possible and became a production line with a capacity figure attached, and the unit being produced is an animal.

properties.name: Ceva Santé Animale
properties.desc: A vectored vaccine is an engineered organism by construction: a gene from one organism is inserted into the genome of a virus, which is then given to the animal alive. This company runs a line of thirteen such vaccines built on fowlpox virus and on herpesvirus of turkeys, carrying antigens for Newcastle disease, infectious bursal disease, infectious laryngotracheitis, avian influenza and Mycoplasma gallisepticum. Its Newcastle product inserts the virus's fusion gene into the turkey herpesvirus genome, with the insertion site and promoter patented. These go into commercial poultry at a scale nothing else on this map approaches, and frequently in ovo — injected into the egg before the bird has hatched. The industry treats them as vaccines and the biosafety literature treats them as recombinant organisms, and both descriptions are accurate at once.

properties.name: Merck Animal Health
properties.state: Rahway, New Jersey — Merck Animal Health
properties.desc: The Innovax line puts the Newcastle disease fusion protein gene into a turkey herpesvirus vector, so a vaccinated bird develops immunity to Marek's disease from the vector itself and to Newcastle from the insert. Later products in the line carry two antigens at once. The reason multi-antigen constructs exist is worth stating plainly, because it is a fact about engineered organisms rather than about marketing: giving a bird two different recombinant herpesvirus vaccines is not recommended, because the faster-replicating one can neutralise the slower and compromise both. Engineered viruses given to the same animal compete with each other, and the industry solved that by combining the inserts rather than by using fewer vectors.

properties.name: Boehringer Ingelheim Animal Health
properties.state: Lyon and Saint-Priest, France — Boehringer Ingelheim Animal Health
properties.desc: The other half of the vectored poultry market: a turkey herpesvirus construct carrying infectious bursal disease antigen, extended to a three-way version adding laryngotracheitis, and a separate fowlpox-vectored line for Newcastle disease and for H5 and H7 avian influenza. Fowlpox-vectored influenza vaccines date to the 1980s, which makes this one of the oldest deliberate uses of a recombinant organism in agriculture anywhere — older than any engineered crop on this map, and almost never counted alongside them. Over a dozen herpesvirus-vectored poultry vaccines are now commercially available across these three companies.

properties.name: European Medicines Agency
properties.desc: A viral vector vaccine falls within the European Union's own definition of a genetically modified organism, and until 2020 that meant an environmental risk assessment and consent under the deliberate release and contained use directives before a clinical trial could proceed. On 15 July 2020 Parliament and Council suspended that requirement for COVID-19 products by regulation: packaging, storage, transport, disposal, distribution, supply and administration in an authorised trial no longer needed the prior assessment or consent, though manufacturing sites and the genetic modification of wild-type viruses stayed inside the contained use rules, and a marketed product still required the assessment. Sponsors were instead obliged to take appropriate measures against foreseeable negative environmental effects of intended or unintended release. Whatever one concludes about the emergency, this is the clearest instance anywhere of a jurisdiction setting aside its own biosafety procedure under time pressure — and of that procedure being described, by its own legislature, as too slow to use when it mattered.

properties.name: Ministério Público Federal — Brasília
properties.desc: In 2013 Brazil's federal public prosecutor opened a civil inquiry into possible illegalities in the biosafety commission's commercial release of soy and maize engineered to tolerate 2,4-D, glyphosate and glufosinate, naming the files then on the commission's agenda and the companies that would benefit from them. The prosecutor also asked the commission to approve no new engineered organisms until in-depth environmental and health studies had been done and a broad public discussion held. The mechanism is what makes it worth carrying: a civil inquiry is opened by a prosecutor on the prosecutor's own initiative, without a claimant, a plaintiff class or anyone who has yet been harmed. Where a country has an office like this, a regulator's decision can be examined by someone who did not have to be injured first to ask.

properties.name: CELMA v. the Intacta approval
properties.state: Buenos Aires — Corte Suprema de Justicia de la Nación
properties.desc: An Argentine environmental law centre complained to the Supreme Court about how a herbicide-tolerant soybean had been approved, on two specific grounds: that the approval had not gone through the public consultation Argentine law requires, and that no environmental impact study had been carried out. The grounds matter more than the outcome. Most challenges to an engineered crop argue about the organism; this one argued about the PROCEDURE, and a procedural defect does not need a scientific dispute to establish. It is the same route the Mexican collective action took to its precautionary measure, and it is available wherever a country's own law promises a consultation it did not hold.

properties.name: Conselho Nacional de Biosegurança (CNBS)
properties.desc: Brazil's 2005 biosafety law restructured the technical commission and created a national biosafety council above it, along with a national biosafety policy. The commission decides on the science; the council sits over it and the commission reports to it. That two-tier design is unusual and worth knowing about wherever an approval is being contested, because it means a technical decision has a political body with authority over it, and civil society objections to the engineered wheat approval have been directed there as well as at the commission. A reader looking for where to object in Brazil needs both addresses, not one.

properties.name: Envigo — Cumberland County breeding facility
properties.desc: A dog-breeding facility supplying research beagles was shut in October 2022 after documented welfare violations. Around four thousand animals were removed, 446 of them in acute distress, and 3,776 were placed for adoption. The conditions recorded included dogs killed by injection to the heart without proper anaesthetic, and survivors with rotting teeth. It belongs on this map for two reasons beyond the animals. First, it is the largest single removal of research animals from a US supplier, and it happened under welfare inspection rather than through any biosafety route. Second, the executives involved reappear: the chief operating officer at the time of those violations later became chief executive of a company proposing a new macaque breeding facility, which is how a community in Georgia came to learn the history of the people asking to build next door.

properties.name: Indian Immunologicals Limited
properties.state: Hyderabad — a subsidiary of the National Dairy Development Board
properties.desc: One of India's largest veterinary vaccine producers, holding roughly a fifth of that national market, and owned by the National Dairy Development Board rather than by private shareholders. It has also worked on human vaccines built by codon de-optimisation — rewriting a virus's genetic code so it replicates poorly while still provoking immunity, which is genetic engineering of a pathogen by any definition, undertaken in a research collaboration with an Australian university. It belongs in this facet because the vaccine industry outside the United States and Europe is largely absent from this map, and because a state-linked producer answers to a different set of pressures than a listed animal health company: its output is priced for a dairy sector rather than for a shareholder.

properties.name: Hester Biosciences
properties.desc: An Indian animal health company holding around fifteen per cent of the national veterinary vaccine market, concentrated in poultry, and with manufacturing in Africa as well as India. Poultry is where recombinant vector vaccines are used at the largest scale anywhere — given in ovo, before the bird hatches — and the producers already on this map are all European or American. A company at this share of one of the world's biggest poultry sectors is a material part of who administers engineered viruses to animals, and its absence would leave that trade looking like a transatlantic one.

properties.name: Biogenesis Bago
properties.desc: An Argentine veterinary vaccine manufacturer named among the principal companies in the global sector, with operations extending into India. It is the only Latin American producer in that group, and it sits in the country that also holds the first engineered wheat, the herbicide-tolerant soy that covers most of its arable land, and the regulator whose gene-editing criteria the rest of the world has copied. The animal health side of that same concentration is rarely counted alongside the crop side, and it is the same few kilometres of the Buenos Aires hinterland.

properties.name: JOINN Laboratories
properties.state: Beijing — with Suzhou, Chongqing, Guangzhou and US sites
properties.desc: Founded in 1995 and listed in both Shanghai and Hong Kong, this is the largest non-clinical safety assessment provider in China: 73,200 square metres of animal experiment facilities across its two main bases alone, holding accreditations against Chinese, US, OECD, Japanese and South Korean good laboratory practice, and expanded into the United States by acquisition. Its dedicated laboratory animal sites sit separately in Wuzhou, Yunnan and Nanning. Two things follow. Safety studies read by regulators worldwide are increasingly produced in a country the reading regulator does not inspect — the accreditations are the substitute for that. And the company moved to secure its own primate breeding capacity when the supply tightened, so the contractor running the study and the supplier of the animals used in it are converging into one firm.

properties.name: ACB v Minister of Agriculture and Monsanto
properties.state: Bloemfontein — Supreme Court of Appeal of South Africa
properties.desc: Nine years of litigation, ended in October 2024 by a full bench of five judges setting aside several layers of decision-making behind the commercial release of drought-tolerant maize MON87460. The permit had been granted in June 2015 and appealed within two months; the High Court dismissed the challenge in 2023 and the Supreme Court of Appeal set that judgment aside too, including its findings on the precautionary principle. The argument was administrative rather than scientific: that the executive council had accepted the applicant's evidence uncritically and disregarded the contrary expert evidence put before it. Three things make this the most useful case on the map for a reader outside Europe and North America — it was brought by a small non-profit with legal aid, it succeeded on how the decision was made rather than on proving harm, and it took nine years, which is the real price of that route.

properties.name: Executive Council: GMO Act (South Africa)
properties.desc: The body that authorises releases in the biggest engineered-crop producer in Africa, sitting under the agriculture department with a separate appeal board above it. It approved open field trials of drought-tolerant maize in 2007, extended them in 2010 and granted commercial release in 2015 — and in 2024 the Supreme Court of Appeal set that chain of decisions aside. Read it alongside the Brazilian council and the Indian committee already on this map: three countries, three different structures for who signs off a release, and in each the interesting question is not the science but who checks the body that checked the applicant.

properties.name: Legal Aid South Africa
properties.desc: The state-funded legal assistance body that represented the non-profit which took the drought-tolerant maize approval to the Supreme Court of Appeal and won. It is on this map because it answers the question every other case entry raises and none of them resolves: who pays for nine years of litigation against a multinational and a government department. Legal standing without funded representation is a right nobody can exercise, and in this instance a publicly funded service is what made the difference between a documented objection and a judgment that set the approval aside.

properties.name: Rallis India
properties.desc: An Indian crop protection and seeds company within the Tata group, running its own research stations and field programmes alongside a seeds business. It sits in the same position as the European agroscience contractors already on this map — generating the agronomic and efficacy data that supports a product through registration — but inside a domestic conglomerate rather than as an independent service. That difference matters for who the data belongs to: an independent contractor sells a study to whoever commissions it, while an in-house programme generates evidence for its own group's products and nobody else sees the ones that did not work.

properties.name: Insect Pest Control Laboratory, Seibersdorf
properties.state: Seibersdorf, Austria — FAO/IAEA Agriculture and Biotechnology Laboratories
properties.desc: The laboratory that supplies the strains, methods and training behind sterile insect programmes worldwide, run jointly by the UN food agency and the atomic energy agency thirty-five kilometres outside Vienna. It works on mass rearing, sterilisation, quality control and genetics for fruit flies, moths, tsetse flies and mosquitoes, and supplies biological material to member states. Its central product is the genetic sexing strain — a line engineered or bred so that only males survive to be released, which matters absolutely for mosquitoes because only females bite. The classic strains for the Mediterranean fruit fly, VIENNA 7 and VIENNA 8, came from here and are used across the world. Work has moved from selective breeding to transposable elements, site-specific recombination and CRISPR editing, and to tetracycline-repressible female-lethal lines. A reader who thinks of released engineered insects as a company's business should know that the strain underneath most programmes comes from a UN laboratory.

properties.name: Joint FAO/IAEA Centre of Nuclear Techniques in Food and Agriculture
properties.desc: The programme that funds and coordinates the research behind the sterile insect technique, running projects with fifteen to twenty member states at a time and publishing the results as journal special issues. It set out to build a generic framework for producing male-only strains applicable across pest species, because the classic fruit fly strains depend on mutations that do not transfer. Its stated position on validation is worth recording: any new genetic sexing strain must be tested under mass-rearing conditions and in small-scale pilot trials before deployment in a large programme. That is an intergovernmental body writing a release protocol for engineered insects, outside the Cartagena machinery that governs everything else on this map.

properties.name: Center for Aquaculture Technologies
properties.state: San Diego, California — 8395 Camino Santa Fe
properties.desc: A contract research and services company founded in 2012 that sells genome editing to fish breeding companies, and holds patents covering the use of editing to induce reproductive sterility and control sex in aquatic species. It states a sterility-first rule: sterility is a precondition for adding any further edits, on the reasoning that farmed fish which reach open water should not be able to breed with wild ones or establish populations. Read that alongside the fluorescent zebrafish now breeding in Brazilian creeks and it is the same problem answered two ways — one by a pond wall, one by editing the animal so the wall matters less. It also sells sex control, because male tilapia and Atlantic salmon grow faster, which is a commercial reason travelling in the same construct as the containment one.

properties.name: Aruna Rodrigues v Union of India
properties.state: New Delhi — Supreme Court of India
properties.desc: A public interest petition filed in 2005 and still running. Its record is the longest continuous judicial supervision of engineered crops anywhere: the Court directed the regulator to withhold approvals in September 2006, lifted that in May 2007 subject to a 200 metre isolation distance around field tests, added a 0.01 per cent level-of-detection protocol in April 2008, appointed an independent expert in 2009, and in 2012 appointed a Technical Expert Committee whose interim report recommended a ten-year moratorium on field trials — which the government rejected as inconclusive. On 23 July 2024 two judges split on the conditional approval of engineered mustard but agreed unanimously that the government must produce a national policy on engineered crops, through consultation with experts and state governments, within four months. A contempt application followed, alleging the policy was not made and releases went ahead anyway. What this case demonstrates is a court substituting itself for a regulator for two decades, and the limits of that: isolation distances and detection thresholds are enforceable orders, a national policy is not.

properties.name: Gene Campaign
properties.desc: An Indian research and advocacy organisation that brought its own petition to the Supreme Court alongside the longer-running one, seeking a halt on environmental release until a transparent biosafety protocol conducted by independent bodies was placed in the public domain. Both petitions were heard together and decided on the same day in July 2024. It belongs on this map because the crop side rarely records who actually files: a court cannot act without a petitioner, and in the country with the world's second largest population and only one commercially approved transgenic crop, the petitioners have been a small number of named individuals and organisations for twenty years.

properties.name: Sala Constitucional de Costa Rica — expediente 12-017013-0007-CO
properties.state: San José — Sala Constitucional de la Corte Suprema de Justicia
properties.desc: In September 2014 the constitutional chamber cancelled the permits granted for planting engineered maize in Costa Rica, ruling for the ecological organisations that had brought the action two years earlier. The route to that judgment is what makes it worth studying. When a Monsanto affiliate obtained permission in January 2013 to plant in Guanacaste, campaigners went to the municipalities rather than only to the courts: within about two years, 75 of the country's 81 cantons had declared themselves territories free of engineered crops, alongside statements against the maize from the governing bodies of all four public universities and from the agronomists' professional college. The legal argument that followed rested partly on municipal autonomy — a national permit to plant inside a canton that had prohibited it. A constitutional court is not usually reachable by a village council, and this is the clearest case on the map of local government being used as the route to one.

properties.name: Federación Costarricense para la Conservación del Ambiente (FECON)
properties.desc: The Costa Rican ecological federation, which holds a seat on the national technical biosafety commission and used it to say publicly that the commission had no intention of changing its permissive practice and would remain a processing department. That is an unusual position to be able to document: a critic inside the body granting the permits, describing how it works, on the record. The federation also organised the municipal declaration campaign that produced the canton-level prohibitions, and argued that a permit issued for land inside a canton with a moratorium could be unconstitutional or at least violate municipal autonomy — the argument that reached the constitutional chamber.

properties.name: Synbio Technologies
properties.state: Monmouth Junction, New Jersey — with operations in Nanjing
properties.desc: A gene synthesis company operating across the United States and China, and a member of the industry's voluntary screening consortium. Its published capability is the reason it belongs here: synthesis to lengths of 200 kilobases, whole small genomes assembled through yeast, and — stated on its own product page — arbitrary synthesis of adenovirus genomes. An adenovirus genome is the backbone of the vector vaccines elsewhere on this map. When the capability to write a viral genome to order is a catalogue item rather than a national programme, the constraint on who can build an engineered organism stops being technical and becomes whatever the screening protocol catches.

properties.name: Afrigen Biologics
properties.desc: Selected in June 2021 by the World Health Organization and the Medicines Patent Pool as the mRNA technology transfer hub, after Moderna and Pfizer declined to provide the know-how to reproduce their vaccines in Africa. Afrigen used the publicly available sequence of Moderna's vaccine to build its own version at laboratory scale — the first vaccine made from a widely used product without the developer's assistance or approval, and the first mRNA vaccine designed and produced on the continent. In 2026 it became the first African facility certified to manufacture investigational biological products for early clinical trials. Its task was to industrialise the platform and transfer it to fifteen partners on four continents. The entry belongs on this map because it is the clearest instance of a genetic technology being rebuilt from a published sequence rather than licensed — the same act the synthesis facet describes as a capability, carried out as policy.

properties.name: Bio-Manguinhos / Fiocruz
properties.state: Rio de Janeiro — Fundação Oswaldo Cruz
properties.desc: The immunobiologicals institute of Brazil's public health foundation, and one of two Latin American partners in the mRNA transfer programme. In 2021 it supplied more than 233 million doses of vaccines, including 153 million doses of a recombinant COVID-19 vaccine produced under a partnership with AstraZeneca. Both halves matter: it manufactures another company's recombinant product at enormous scale under licence, and it is simultaneously learning to build an mRNA platform it would own. A state manufacturer that is both licensee and would-be developer is a different actor from either a multinational or a contract manufacturer, and this map has very few of them.

properties.name: Sinergium Biotech
properties.desc: The private Argentine biopharmaceutical company that is the other Latin American partner in the mRNA transfer programme, working at pilot scale on the platform developed in Cape Town. It sits in the same industrial corridor north of Buenos Aires as the country's veterinary vaccine manufacturing, which is worth noticing: human and animal recombinant production, the first engineered wheat and the regulator that wrote the gene-editing criteria others copied are all within a short distance of each other, and this map has generally recorded them as though they were separate industries.

properties.name: ABS Global
properties.state: DeForest, Wisconsin — a Genus plc company
properties.desc: A bovine genetics company founded in 1941, operating in seventy countries, and the arm through which its listed parent sells sex-sorted semen under the Sexcel brand. Sorting sperm by sex is not gene editing, and this facet should say so plainly — but it is the same industrial decision at one remove: which part of a herd passes on its genetics, and whether the calf is born male or female, chosen at the point of insemination. Sexed doses retail at roughly three to five times the price of conventional ones. The company also owns a Brazilian bovine IVF business outright. A reader following engineered livestock will find the editing companies elsewhere on this map; the firms that already decide which animals reproduce are these, and they were here first.

properties.name: Semex Alliance
properties.desc: A Canadian cattle genetics organisation owned by its member breeders rather than by shareholders, and one of the small group that dominates bovine artificial insemination worldwide alongside the listed and cooperative firms in Europe and North America. It owns its own reproductive technology company, which is the pattern worth recording across this facet: the same firms now control both the sorting technology and the genetic catalogues, so a farmer buying semen is buying from an organisation that owns both halves and can no longer be played against a rival on either.

properties.name: URUS Group
properties.desc: A holding company that brings several cattle breeding and reproduction brands under one owner, including Alta Genetics, GENEX and an embryo transfer business, with operations across North America, Latin America and beyond. Consolidation in this facet is quieter than in seed and has had far less attention, but the shape is the same: a farmer choosing between what look like competing brands of bull semen, embryo services and herd management software may be choosing among subsidiaries of one group.

properties.name: Nuziveedu Seeds
properties.desc: India's largest domestic seed company, founded in 1973, and the licensee that fought its licensor to a standstill. It took a Bt cotton licence from the Monsanto joint venture in 2004 for an initial ten years, on a recurring trait-value payment; when state governments began capping seed prices and the licensor would not reduce the fee, the Indian companies stopped paying, the licence was terminated, and litigation ran from 2015 to a settlement in March 2021, passing through the Delhi High Court twice, an arbitration and the Supreme Court. Alongside it the agriculture ministry set a national price for engineered cotton seed and the royalty allowed on it, and asked the competition authority to investigate the licensor. Its chairman was simultaneously president of the national seed association — the same person leading the company, the trade body and the public argument. This is the clearest case on the map of a licensee with enough domestic weight to change the terms of a trait licence rather than accept them.

properties.name: Kaveri Seed Company
properties.desc: Founded in 1976 and among the largest Indian seed companies, concentrated in cotton and maize hybrids across the south and centre of the country, with a research programme of its own rather than a purely distributive business. It sits in the group of domestic firms that sub-licensed engineered cotton traits from the multinational joint venture and then found the terms of that licence contested in court and capped by government. Reading this facet, the useful distinction is between a company that owns a trait and a company that owns the hybrid it is crossed into — in India the second group is large, organised and politically effective, which is not the case in most countries on this map.

properties.name: Rasi Seeds
properties.desc: One of the Indian hybrid seed companies holding sub-licences to engineered cotton traits, with a portfolio across cotton, maize, paddy, millet, sunflower and vegetables and a national dealer network. Its presence matters to the shape of this facet rather than to any single event: engineered cotton reached millions of Indian smallholders through a dozen or so domestic hybrid companies like this one, not through the trait owner's own brand. The trait travelled on somebody else's seed, which is why a dispute over royalties between two companies became a national price-control question.

properties.name: Advanta Seeds
properties.desc: Established in 1994 and now inside the UPL group, breeding rice, maize, sorghum and mustard aimed at low-input and high-risk growing areas, and operating well beyond India. The position is worth recording because this map documents mostly the opposite kind of company: a seed business owned by a crop protection multinational, selling into the smallholder segment that the four majors have generally not served directly. Whether that is a route into a market or a route out of dependence on it is exactly the question this facet exists to let a reader ask.

properties.name: Seed Co Group
properties.state: Harare — international headquarters in South Africa
properties.desc: Africa's largest home-grown seed company, founded in 1940 as the Seed Maize Association of Zimbabwe by farmers wanting reliable maize seed, now operating across roughly twenty African countries with maize, soya, wheat, sorghum, groundnuts, cotton, rice and vegetables, and running the largest single out-grower scheme in the seed business. Limagrain — the largest seed and plant breeding company in the European Union — bought in from 2014 and holds around 30 per cent, and the vegetable seed line is distributed with a Limagrain business unit. It also sold 49 per cent of Africa's only cottonseed company to an Indian firm part-owned by Monsanto. A farmer cooperative that became a continental company and then a partly foreign-owned one is the whole trajectory of this facet in a single organisation.

properties.name: Quton Seed Company
properties.desc: Described at the time of its sale as Africa's only cottonseed company, and notable for producing open-pollinated varieties as well as hybrids — seed a farmer can save and replant. In 2014 a 49 per cent stake was sold to an Indian seed company that is part-owned by Monsanto and holds a joint venture to sub-license engineered cotton traits across India. The detail that matters is the difference in what each side breeds: the buyer specialises in hybrid cotton, which must be repurchased every season. Whether open-pollinated lines survive a change of ownership is a question this map can only answer by recording who owns them.

properties.name: knoell
properties.state: Mannheim, Germany — with offices in the US, UK and Asia
properties.desc: A regulatory consultancy that writes the submissions. Its published service list includes dossier preparation for the European food safety authority in the required electronic format, US federal and state pesticide registration, study management and monitoring, and — named explicitly — agronomic equivalence evaluation, meaning the comparison of an engineered plant against conventional varieties. It also selects which laboratory performs a study, with the stated aim of producing data usable for submissions in more than one country. That is the mechanism this facet exists to show: the same firm can design the study, choose the laboratory, interpret the result and write the argument the regulator reads, and none of those steps is hidden — they are the product being sold.

properties.name: Fera Science
properties.state: Sand Hutton, York — a joint venture with the UK government
properties.desc: The former UK Food and Environment Research Agency, now a joint venture in which the government retains a stake alongside a private partner, selling laboratory and field services and regulatory consultancy. Its own pitch is the notable part: it offers established working relationships with competent authorities as a reason to hire it. A body that was the state's own science agency, now selling access to the regulator's confidence as a commercial service, is a different object from either a government laboratory or an independent contractor, and this map has almost no other examples of the type.

properties.name: NIAB
properties.desc: A century-old British crop research organisation running industry-funded field trials: early plant breeding screens, disease assessment, agrochemical evaluation for the registration of new products, and demonstration plots for farmers. It states plainly that all such work is strictly confidential. That single condition is why the trial layer of this map is thin in Europe — the plots exist, the data exists, and a member of the public cannot see either, because the contract rather than the regulation determines what is published.

properties.name: Battelle
properties.desc: A large non-profit research institute with a crop protection practice covering regulatory affairs, dossier preparation and field-based measurement of how sprayed material moves and settles. Its staff biographies describe carrying techniques developed for defence work into agricultural clients. It belongs here because it is the least commercial-looking organisation in this facet and does the same work: a non-profit institute preparing regulatory submissions for industry is still preparing them for the applicant, and the reader should not read the tax status as independence.

properties.name: Instituto Mato-Grossense do Algodão (IMAmt)
properties.state: Primavera do Leste, Mato Grosso — experimental station
properties.desc: A non-profit research institute created in 2007 by the members of the Mato Grosso cotton growers' association, and described by that association as its technological arm. It runs a cotton breeding programme aimed at yield, fibre quality and resistance to the diseases and nematodes of the region, a molecular biology laboratory at its experimental station, a network of trials across the state's cotton districts, and a plant protection department testing fungicides, herbicides and insecticides. Its published cultivar comparisons sit alongside the transgenic events sold by the multinationals. This is the third model in this facet: not an independent contractor selling studies, not a state institute, but a laboratory owned by the growers whose crop is being tested — which changes who the results are for.

properties.name: Instituto Agronômico de Campinas (IAC)
properties.desc: One of the oldest agricultural research institutes in the Americas, run by the state of São Paulo, breeding cultivars and running the trials that establish how a genotype behaves under local pathogens and pests — including collaborative work with the producer-funded cotton institute in Mato Grosso on a virus affecting the crop. It matters to this map because Brazil's field research capacity is split three ways: a federal corporation, state institutes like this one, and grower-funded foundations, with the multinationals' own trials on top. A reader trying to find who tested a variety before it reached the market has four different kinds of answer to check, and only one of them is the company that sells it.

properties.name: Associação Mato-grossense dos Produtores de Algodão (AMPA)
properties.desc: The cotton producers' association of Mato Grosso, Brazil's largest cotton state, which created and funds the research institute that breeds the varieties its members grow and tests the chemicals they buy. A trade association that owns its own research capacity is unusual on this map: most of the associations recorded here lobby and publish, while the testing is done by contractors or by the state. Where growers fund the trials, the studies answer to the people planting the crop rather than to the company selling the trait — which is a genuinely different arrangement, whatever one concludes about the results.

properties.name: CryoArks
properties.state: Cardiff University — hubs in London and Edinburgh
properties.desc: A research-council-funded consortium of museums, zoos, universities and biobanks that built the United Kingdom's first comprehensive zoological biobank, linking millions of samples that were sitting in disconnected collections. Its two main storage hubs are the Natural History Museum in London and National Museums Scotland in Edinburgh; capacity runs to roughly a quarter of a million samples across freezers at minus eighty and liquid nitrogen. The point of the project is not storage but a common web portal and common standards, so a researcher can find out what exists. Two consequences worth holding: the material includes samples from wild populations and from species that are now extinct, and a stated aim is to reduce destructive sampling of permanent museum specimens by giving researchers something else to cut into.

properties.name: EAZA Biobank
properties.state: Amsterdam — European Association of Zoos and Aquaria
properties.desc: The biobanking service for the European and Middle Eastern zoo and aquarium association, operating through national hubs rather than one central store — the United Kingdom hub sits in a purpose-built facility at Edinburgh Zoo with capacity for a further eighty thousand specimens. It is the institutional counterpart to the seed vaults on the crop side of this map: a network of captive-animal collections systematically preserving tissue, blood, serum, DNA and cell lines from the animals in their care. Whether that material is a conservation resource or a supply of starting material for the de-extinction ventures elsewhere in this facet is not decided by the biobank — it is decided by whoever is granted a loan from it.

properties.name: Royal Zoological Society of Scotland — WildGenes
properties.desc: A conservation genetics laboratory inside a zoo, and the point where two biobanking networks meet: it is simultaneously a CryoArks storage hub and the United Kingdom hub of the European zoo association's biobank, holding up to forty thousand frozen samples per ultra-cold freezer and processing donations and outgoing loan requests. It is worth recording because the practical questions in this facet are logistical rather than philosophical: who accepts a sample, on what terms, who may request it later, and who does the freezing. The answers here are a charity, a shared standard and two freezers in Edinburgh.

properties.name: Global Genome Biodiversity Network
properties.state: Washington DC — an international network of biorepositories
properties.desc: An international network of institutions holding genomic samples representing the diversity of non-human life, and the layer above the national biobanks: the standards body and index rather than a store. Its existence answers a question this map keeps running into — an engineered crop event carries an OECD identifier that follows it across borders, while a wild tissue sample generally carries only whatever the holding institution wrote down. A network that agrees common records for biodiversity samples is doing for wild genetic material what the identifier system did for commercial events, and it is doing it voluntarily rather than under a treaty.

properties.name: Lohmann Tierzucht
properties.state: Cuxhaven, Germany — an EW Group company
properties.desc: The market leader in white egg layer genetics, and one of three layer brands inside the same German family holding company alongside Hy-Line International and H&N. Almost every white egg eaten anywhere descends from a handful of closed breeding lines, and those lines are the asset: a commercial farm buys parent stock and cannot breed replacements from it, because the performance comes from crossing lines the farm does not hold. That is the same structure as a hybrid seed and it long predates any engineered organism — which is exactly why it belongs on a map about who controls reproduction.

properties.name: Hy-Line International
properties.state: Des Moines, Iowa — an EW Group company
properties.desc: A layer breeding company owned by the same German group as the German and American layer brands beside it, distributing breeding stock into more than a hundred countries. The concentration is the entry rather than the company: by one 2022 estimate the group holds around 44 per cent of the international broiler genetics market through its broiler subsidiary while also leading layer genetics through this business and two others. A reader who has followed the seed facet's four majors should note that poultry is more concentrated still, and attracts a fraction of the attention.

properties.name: Institut de Sélection Animale (ISA)
properties.state: Boxmeer, Netherlands — a Hendrix Genetics company
properties.desc: The layer breeding arm of the Dutch multispecies breeding group, and the leading supplier of brown egg genetics, sold under a set of brand names that look like separate companies and are not. The group also breeds pigs, turkeys and farmed fish. Between it and the German holding company, essentially all commercial turkey and egg-laying stock and most meat chicken stock in the world originates from two corporations — a degree of concentration this map records nowhere else, including in seed.

properties.name: DanBred
properties.desc: The Danish pig breeding organisation, historically owned through the farmers' meat cooperative and among the largest suppliers of pig genetics worldwide. It is on this map as the cooperative case in a facet otherwise made of listed companies and family holdings: the pig genetics market is led by a British listed company and a Dutch group, and the fourth of the top four grew out of a producers' cooperative. Whether a cooperative behaves differently once it competes at that scale is the question a reader can carry to the Canadian cattle organisation and the Brazilian cotton institute elsewhere in these entries.

properties.name: Chinese Academy of Forestry — State Key Laboratory of Tree Genetics and Breeding
properties.desc: Where the world's first commercialised engineered tree came from. Work began in the late 1980s, a Bt gene was put into black poplar in 1989, field testing followed in 1994, and the State Forestry Administration approved two clones for commercial planting in 2002 and 2003 — the first anywhere. Roughly 1.4 million trees went into 300 to 500 hectares; a 2016 count put the area at 543 hectares. The target was the beetle damage running through China's 7 million hectares of clonal poplar. The programme was assisted between 1990 and 1995 by an FAO project funded through the UN development programme, and by a long working relationship with a German federal forestry research centre. An engineered forest tree in commercial ground for two decades is the single most informative thing in this facet, and it is not in North America or Europe.

properties.name: Institute of Forest Biotechnology, Agricultural University of Hebei
properties.desc: The laboratory that has published the longest-running field studies on the commercialised poplar, including a five-year assessment of effects on the arthropod community and soil bacteria around transgenic 741 poplar. Its reviews state the position plainly: nearly 22 insect-resistant poplar varieties have been approved for small-scale testing, environmental release or pilot production; efficacy differs between clones, larval stages and insect species; and expression of one Bt protein was significantly higher than another and varied with developmental stage and tissue. A perennial with a long growth cycle needs long-term assessment before commercial production — and here the commercialisation came first and the five-year study afterwards.

properties.name: Nanjing Institute of Environmental Sciences
properties.desc: The environmental research institute that reported finding genes from the engineered poplars in natural poplar varieties — despite the official position that the commercialised clones were female with altered fertility, which was the reason given for expecting no cross-breeding. A forestry academy official separately observed that the true area of engineered plantation cannot be assessed, because poplar is easy to propagate and sell, material moves between nurseries, and an engineered tree cannot be told from a conventional one by looking at it. Those two findings together are the clearest documented case on this map of a containment assumption failing and the record of where the organism went failing with it.

properties.name: Suprema Corte de Justicia de la Nación — surrogacy, 2021
properties.desc: In 2021 Mexico's supreme court held surrogacy to be a protected medical procedure under the constitutional right to form a family, and to be equally accessible regardless of gender, marital status or sexual orientation. The ruling upheld a surrogate's right to be compensated and displaced state-level restrictions, including one state's exclusion of foreigners. The effect was the opposite of every other movement recorded in this facet: while Thailand, Nepal, India, Cambodia and Russia were closing to foreign intended parents and Georgia was announcing the same, a constitutional court opened a jurisdiction. Only two states have since passed explicit regulations, so elsewhere in the country the arrangement runs through individual court orders — a right established nationally and administered case by case.

properties.name: Kheiron Biotech
properties.desc: The Argentine laboratory that turned horse cloning into a working industry and then moved past it. It produced eight clones of a single high-value polo mare in 2016, one of the first successful multiple clonings of a performance horse. The animal cost is on the record: of 38 live births from its first clones between 2012 and 2016, made from adult skin cells, almost half had abnormalities of the umbilical cord or placenta, or abnormally bent limbs; results improved when the laboratory switched to bone marrow stem cells. In 2024 it produced five gene-edited foals using CRISPR, based on the genome of a hall-of-fame mare and edited for speed — its scientific director describing the work as designing their genome before they are born. It also states work on pigs for organ transplant compatibility and on cattle for higher protein and shorter coats. Cloning to editing, in one company, in one decade.

properties.name: Crestview Genetics
properties.desc: The company founded to clone one polo player's horses, after tissue was preserved from a mare that had to be put down following a fracture in a tournament final in 2006. It partnered with a Texas cloning firm to do the work, and the first foals were born in 2010. At the end of that year a clone of the player's flagship mare sold at auction for a reported $800,000. This is the clearest illustration in the facet of what drives the market: not agricultural yield, not conservation, but the resale value of a copy of a single exceptional animal — and a sport whose governing bodies had to decide afterwards whether the copies could compete.

properties.name: Gemini Genetics
properties.desc: One of the United Kingdom's first animal tissue banks, founded in 2018, taking skin samples from dogs, cats and horses and culturing and cryopreserving them so the cells stay able to regenerate rather than merely intact. The cloning itself happens in Texas: samples are shipped to a US partner when an owner decides to proceed, with an option to hold material in both countries at once. That division of labour is the entry. The step that is time-critical and must happen near the animal — taking and culturing the tissue — is done locally and is not itself cloning; the regulated act happens on another continent. Its sister companies are a stallion insemination service and a kennel fertility clinic, and it also supports a conservation biobank on this map. Pet, livestock and endangered-species genetics run through one small Shropshire operation.

properties.name: Elite Kennel Fertility
properties.desc: A canine fertility clinic, and the sister company through which tissue reaches the tissue bank next door. Its own explanation of why tissue rather than sperm or eggs is the clearest statement of the technical case in this facet: semen freezing is widely available but only for entire males, egg freezing is limited, castrated animals are excluded altogether, and sex cells carry half the DNA of body cells. Skin tissue sidesteps all four constraints. That is why the pet cloning industry is built on tissue banks rather than on the reproductive services that came before it, and why a service sold as preservation is the necessary first half of a service sold as cloning.

properties.name: Waitangi Tribunal — Wai 262 (Ko Aotearoa Tēnei)
properties.desc: Filed in 1991 by members of six iwi and reported on 2 July 2011 — twenty years — in a document of more than a thousand pages, the tribunal's first whole-of-government report, addressing around twenty departments, agencies and Crown entities. Chapter 2 deals directly with the genetic and biological resources of taonga species, and the recommendations fall in three areas: bioprospecting, genetic modification, and intellectual property including patents and plant variety rights. Two findings are worth carrying to any jurisdiction. The tribunal held that kaitiaki do NOT have a right of ownership over taonga species, but that the kaitiaki relationship requires protection in its own right — which is a different legal claim from ownership and available where ownership is not. And the recommendations are NOT binding on the Crown, which is why this appears on a map of industry rather than of law: the finding was made, published in full, and left to be adopted or not.

properties.name: Ngāti Kuri, Ngāti Wai, Te Rarawa, Ngāti Porou, Ngāti Kahungunu and Ngāti Koata
properties.state: Aotearoa New Zealand — the six claimant iwi
properties.desc: The six iwi whose members lodged the claim in 1991 and pursued it for two decades. All six original claimant representatives died before the process concluded, and a sense of unfinished business has persisted since the report. This map records petitioners as well as tribunals because a finding requires someone willing to spend twenty years obtaining it, and the cost is not usually written down anywhere. Set beside the nine-year South African case, the twenty-year Indian petition and the two-year Costa Rican action, the pattern is consistent: the timescale of a challenge to genetic technology is measured in decades, and the technology moves considerably faster.

properties.name: In re Syngenta AG MIR162 Corn Litigation
properties.state: District of Kansas — federal multidistrict litigation
properties.desc: The company was approved to sell the MIR162 trait in the United States in 2010 and began selling it in 2011, before China had approved it for import. In 2013 the trait appeared in shipments to China, China rejected US corn, and prices fell. The farmers who sued had not planted the trait: their claim was that assurances about imminent Chinese approval were false and that the resulting market closure cost them money. Tens of thousands of suits were consolidated in Kansas federal court; a jury awarded about $218 million to some 7,300 growers in 2017; and in December 2018 a settlement of $1.51 billion was approved, described by the lead attorneys as the largest agricultural litigation settlement in United States history, affecting over 600,000 producers, grain handlers and ethanol plants. The company denied wrongdoing throughout and noted the traits were fully approved by all US authorities at launch — which was true, and is the point. Every other case on this map asks whether a release was safe. This one establishes that a release lawful at home can be actionable because another country had not yet approved it.

properties.name: Cargill and Archer Daniels Midland — the exporters' separate claims
properties.state: Minnetonka and Chicago — the grain exporters
properties.desc: The two largest grain traders were suing the same company over the same events and were expressly excluded from the farmers' settlement, pursuing their claims separately. That separation is the entry. When an unapproved trait reaches an export market, the loss lands on at least three groups with different interests — farmers who never planted it, handlers and ethanol plants who moved it, and the exporters whose cargoes were turned away — and they do not litigate together. A reader tracing who bears the cost of a premature release should expect to find several separate actions rather than one, and the farmers' class is usually the slowest and the largest.

properties.name: Bader Farms, Inc. v. Monsanto Company and BASF Corporation
properties.state: Cape Girardeau — US District Court, Eastern District of Missouri
properties.desc: Missouri's largest peach farm sued over dicamba drift, and in February 2020 a jury awarded $15 million in compensatory and $250 million in punitive damages — the first US jury verdict for property damage to a neighbouring landowner from dicamba drift. The punitive award was reduced to $60 million later that year, and in July 2022 the Eighth Circuit upheld liability while ordering a new trial on punitive damages. The claim was not about the herbicide alone. It was that dicamba-tolerant soybean and cotton seed had been released knowing the accompanying herbicide would move off target onto crops that could not tolerate it. The farm's harvest fell from around 162,000 bushels in the early 2000s to as low as 12,000 in 2018, and it said it would inevitably close. The companies denied the allegations and attributed the damage to illegal applications by other farmers, weather and disease. However that dispute is resolved, the structure is what this map should record: a tolerance trait creates a market for the matching herbicide, and the cost of it landing elsewhere falls on whoever did not buy either.

properties.name: Bader Farms
properties.desc: The peach farm that filed the first dicamba drift lawsuit against the seed company in 2016, and became the bellwether trial for a multidistrict litigation that has drawn in over a hundred farmers, with a crop damage class action and a separate antitrust complaint running alongside it. It is on this map for a reason the case reports do not state plainly: the farm was not a customer of the technology at issue, had no contract with either company, and grew a crop the trait was never designed for. A bellwether plaintiff in this field is often someone with no commercial relationship to the industry at all — which is who ends up carrying the burden of establishing whether a release was negligent.

properties.name: Arkansas State Plant Board
properties.desc: A state regulator that restricted a federally approved product, and was sued for it. After nearly a thousand complaints in 2017 — affecting some 800,000 acres of soybeans alone — it halted in-crop dicamba use by emergency order in July, then voted to bar it from 16 April to 31 October 2018. It held seventeen meetings on the herbicide that year. It also rejected the company's petition, and rejected a further petition seeking to disqualify a board member who represented the state seed growers' association and had solicited support for the cutoff date; he said openly that he saw it as part of representing seed growers. Later boards moved the cutoff to 25 May. The entry matters because sub-national regulators are almost absent from this map, and here one set the binding constraint on a product two federal agencies had approved.

properties.name: Monsanto Co. v. Arkansas State Plant Board
properties.state: Little Rock — Pulaski County Circuit Court and the Supreme Court of Arkansas
properties.desc: The company sued the state board in October 2017, arguing it had exceeded its delegated authority, had failed to consider the research submitted to federal regulators, and that the statute creating the board was an unconstitutional delegation of power. A group of Arkansas farmers sued separately over the same rules. The circuit court dismissed the company's case on sovereign immunity in February 2018; the state supreme court held in 2019 that the claims could be brought, by which time the contested rules had expired and been replaced, so those parts were dismissed as moot while the constitutional question and the research requirement went back down. Two things are visible here that appear nowhere else on this map: a company litigating against a regulator rather than the reverse, and a rule surviving simply by expiring before the challenge concluded.

properties.name: Vaxxinova
properties.desc: A veterinary vaccine company built around autogenous vaccines — vaccines made from pathogens isolated on one particular farm, for that farm, on a veterinarian's prescription, rather than licensed for general sale. It also sells a patented technology that raises antibodies against the iron-transport proteins of bacteria, starving them of an essential nutrient. Autogenous production belongs on this map because of what it does to the record: a product made for a single herd from a locally isolated organism does not go through the approval process a licensed vaccine does, so it appears in no national register of authorised products. The organism is engineered or selected, administered to livestock, and effectively invisible to the registers this map is otherwise built from.

properties.name: HIPRA
properties.state: Amer, Catalonia — with plants in Spain and Brazil
properties.desc: A Spanish animal health company founded in 1971, present in forty countries with subsidiaries and distributing to more than a hundred, running autogenous vaccine plants in Spain and Brazil including a service for farmed fish. In 2020 it crossed into human medicine and developed Spain's first domestic COVID-19 vaccine — an adjuvanted recombinant protein built on a receptor binding domain fusion heterodimer carrying two variants. The crossing is the entry. Recombinant protein production for livestock and for people is the same industrial capability, and a veterinary company was able to move into human vaccines inside two years. This map generally separates the animal and human facets; the manufacturers do not.

properties.name: Bioneeds India
properties.desc: A preclinical contract research organisation on a five-acre campus outside Bengaluru with around 250,000 square feet of built space, plus separate chemistry and biopharma laboratories. It states more than 23,500 good laboratory practice studies submitted to regulators worldwide over sixteen years, breeds its own rats, mice, guinea pigs and rabbits, and is certified under India's national GLP authority, approved by the national animal experiments committee, and accredited by the international laboratory animal care body. Its client range covers pharmaceuticals, vaccines, biologics, medical devices, agrochemicals and industrial chemicals — the same facility producing the safety data behind a crop protection product and a gene therapy. Regulators in a dozen countries read those studies; none of them inspects this campus, and the accreditations are what stands in place of that.

properties.name: Vipragen Biosciences
properties.desc: An end-to-end preclinical contract research organisation serving pharmaceutical, biotechnology, veterinary, nutraceutical and herbal clients in India and abroad, with a vivarium holding OECD good laboratory practice, national testing accreditation and international laboratory animal care accreditation since 2013. It works to the guideline sets of the US food and drug administration, the US environmental protection agency, the World Health Organization and five pharmacopoeias, and it has agreements with a European regulatory consultancy and with Indian medical and scientific institutes. The detail worth keeping is the breadth of the standards list: a mid-sized Indian laboratory holds accreditation to more regulatory regimes than most of the regulators on this map hold jurisdictions.

properties.name: Scion — New Zealand Forest Research Institute
properties.desc: The Crown research institute running what its own page calls the only plant GM field trial currently operating in New Zealand, on a four-hectare containment site approved in 2010 and continuing to 2035. It has been field-testing engineered pine since around 1996. The controls are the most specific on this map: trees must be felled at eight years or as soon as they begin to develop reproductive structures, inspections must find male catkins or female cones soon after they form, and those must be removed within 24 hours and destroyed. Its published annual reports record each transfer from glasshouse to field by date and permit number, and the ministry audits. Whatever one concludes about the research, this is the clearest documented example of what containment actually consists of — people walking a plot looking for cones — and it is worth setting against the Chinese poplar entry where nobody could say how much had been planted.

properties.name: Scion — gene-edited conifer programme
properties.desc: The same institute launched what it describes as the world's first field trial of a gene-edited conifer, using CRISPR to switch off single genes in the pine genome to study wood development, with two sets of trees each carrying a different gene turned off. Separately it has edited Douglas-fir reproductive genes to produce trees that grow normally but cannot reproduce — aimed at New Zealand's wilding conifer problem, where planted forest species spread beyond their plantations into native ecosystems. The proposal is that sterile trees could act as a form of biocontrol for future engineered trees. Note what that means: the answer to trees spreading is a tree engineered not to spread, which is the same reasoning the aquaculture facet uses for sterile fish, arrived at independently in a different kingdom.

properties.name: Leibniz Institute for Zoo and Wildlife Research (Leibniz-IZW)
properties.desc: The institute leading the consortium attempting to prevent the extinction of the northern white rhinoceros. Two females survive, a mother and daughter at a Kenyan conservancy, neither able to carry a pregnancy; living cells from twelve individuals are held in liquid nitrogen. In September 2023 the team achieved the first pregnancy in any rhinoceros after embryo transfer, using a southern white rhino embryo and surrogate — a technique routine in cattle and never before attempted in this family. The surrogate died of a clostridial infection resurfaced by heavy rains; the foetus was 70 days and 6.4 cm, and DNA analysis in January 2024 confirmed it came from the transfer. Twenty-one egg collections from the surviving daughter have produced 38 pure northern white rhino embryos; three transfers of those in late 2025 did not become lasting pregnancies. This is the honest version of what this facet promises: a decade of work, a proof of concept, and no calf yet.

properties.name: Avantea
properties.desc: The Italian laboratory where the rhino embryos are actually made. Eggs collected in Kenya are flown to Cremona, fertilised by intracytoplasmic sperm injection using frozen semen from dead males, and grown to blastocysts there. It is a commercial reproductive biotechnology laboratory whose ordinary business is cattle and horses, and the transfer of that capability to a wild species is the reason the programme exists at all. Note the geography this creates: the animals are in Kenya, the embryos are made in Italy, the stem cell work is in Japan and Germany, and the consortium is coordinated from Czechia. The last two individuals of a subspecies are the subject of a supply chain.

properties.name: Ol Pejeta Conservancy
properties.desc: The Kenyan conservancy where the last two northern white rhinos live, guarded and cared for day and night, and where the egg collections and embryo transfers take place with the national wildlife service and the wildlife research and training institute. It belongs on this map because the biotechnology facets here rarely record the place the animal is: laboratories, funders and consortium leads are documented, and the conservancy holding the last two individuals of a subspecies is treated as a location rather than a party. It is a party — the procedures happen on its ground, under Kenyan authority, and any reintroduction would be to a range it borders.

properties.name: Qiming Venture Partners
properties.state: Shanghai — Jin Mao Tower, with Beijing, Suzhou, Hong Kong and Singapore
properties.desc: Founded in 2006 and managing around $9.5 billion across eleven dollar funds and seven renminbi funds, investing in technology, consumer and healthcare companies with more than 500 investments made. Its healthcare portfolio includes gene editing companies working on genetic disease and mRNA drug developers, and in 2017 it launched a US team and fund of its own. Two structural points: a fund running parallel dollar and renminbi vehicles can take money from foreign and domestic investors into different pools with different rules, which is how Chinese biotechnology has been financed from both directions at once; and a Chinese venture firm raising in the United States is the reverse of the flow this map usually records.

properties.name: Lilly Asia Ventures
properties.state: Shanghai — with Hong Kong and Palo Alto
properties.desc: A biomedical venture firm with roughly $4.5 billion under management, investing in biopharmaceuticals, medical technologies and diagnostics from seed to public stages across Asia and the United States. It began in 2008 as the corporate venture arm of a US pharmaceutical company and was spun out as an independent manager in 2011. That history is the entry. A corporate venture arm invests for strategic reasons as well as financial ones; an independent fund does not. This one was the first and became the second, while keeping the name — which is a useful reminder that the label on a fund describes its origin rather than its current obligations.

properties.name: Ifakara Health Institute
properties.desc: The Tanzanian institute where the first transgenic mosquito ever made in Africa was created, in 2023, as part of a programme co-led with Imperial College London and the national medical research institute.
