The strain expresses antimicrobial peptides derived from frogs and honeybees in the mosquito midgut, triggered when the insect takes a blood meal, and a 2025 study reported it blocking development of the main African malaria parasite using parasites from local patients rather than laboratory strains. The order of events is what this facet needs recorded: the method was developed in London, then rebuilt in Tanzania by Tanzanian scientists trained for it, under Tanzanian institutional and national oversight. Every other gene drive programme on this map is run from the country that will not host the release.

properties.name: Transmission Zero
properties.state: London — Imperial College, with Tanzanian and Swiss partners
properties.desc: Established in 2016 to build a two-part technology: a modification that stops a mosquito transmitting the malaria parasite, and a gene drive to carry that trait through the wild population without killing it. That second half is the distinction worth holding — most engineered mosquito programmes on this map suppress a population, and this one replaces a trait within it, which means the mosquitoes remain and the disease transmission does not. Its own stated position on pace is unusually candid: move at the right speed, not too fast, make sure people are supportive, and still treat malaria as the emergency it is. Further research, risk assessment, regulatory engagement and community consultation are all stated as preceding any field trial.

properties.name: Kilobaser
properties.desc: An Austrian company selling a benchtop DNA and RNA synthesiser — a machine rather than a service. It ships in a wooden crate weighing about 27 kilograms, runs on nitrogen or argon gas, produces custom oligos in under two hours at 2.5 minutes a base, and can be operated entirely offline, which the company presents as a data security feature. Its customers include laboratories in Brazil, India and elsewhere. The reason this belongs beside the gene synthesis companies rather than among them: those companies screen the sequences they are asked to make and check who is ordering, and that screening works because the order has to pass through them. A machine on a bench removes that step entirely. Analyses cited by the industry itself suggest benchtop capacity could reach a tenth to a fifth of total gene synthesis within a decade.

properties.name: Bureau of Industry and Security — commerce control list
properties.state: Washington DC — US Department of Commerce
properties.desc: Partly or fully automated nucleic acid assemblers and synthesisers capable of more than 1.5 kilobases sit on this bureau's control list and on the Australia Group list, and those export controls are, according to arms control analysts, the only consistently applied regulation of benchtop synthesis devices anywhere. Several US bills to require screening of synthesis products have been introduced since 2023 and none has moved past introduction. The position this leaves is worth stating flatly: the machines are controlled as EXPORTS, which governs where they may be sold, while what is synthesised on one already sold is governed by nothing binding. That is the same shape as the gamete courier and the grain shipment elsewhere on this map — a rule attached to crossing a border rather than to the act itself.

properties.name: Shin Nippon Biomedical Laboratories (SNBL)
properties.state: Kagoshima, Japan — with Tokyo, Wakayama, the US, Europe, China and Cambodia
properties.desc: Japan's first contract research organisation, with more than sixty years of work and a specialisation in non-human primate studies that is its stated competitive edge. Its published locations include a laboratory in Phnom Penh. Non-clinical contracts reached the order of tens of billions of yen with overseas orders around 39 per cent of the total, and it has been building a domestic primate breeding system precisely because the imported supply became uncertain — its own risk disclosures name potential Cambodian export restrictions. Set that beside the Chinese safety-assessment company doing the same thing and the pattern is unmistakable: when a supply chain came under legal scrutiny, the contractors did not stop using the animals; they moved to breeding their own. The firm has also had Animal Welfare Act violations recorded at a US site.

properties.name: China Animal Husbandry Industry Co. (CAHIC)
properties.desc: A state-backed producer and, on one 2015 measure, the largest single share of the Chinese animal vaccine market. Its portfolio covers the diseases the state designates as priorities — foot-and-mouth, highly pathogenic avian influenza, classical swine fever — and its government relationships, national distribution and production scale are what make it structural rather than merely large. The mechanism worth carrying: China divides animal vaccines into compulsory and market-priced categories, and the compulsory list is set by the state. A government deciding which diseases must be vaccinated against is deciding the size of a market, and this is the company positioned to serve it.

properties.name: Jinyu Bio-Technology
properties.desc: One of the largest producers of animal vaccines in China and among the homegrown companies that dominate a market foreign firms have struggled to enter. The market's shape is set by policy rather than by demand: porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome and hog cholera were removed from compulsory vaccination in 2017, which moved them into the higher-margin market-priced category, and African swine fever then collapsed the pig herd and with it the hog vaccine share. A company in this position is exposed to two things at once — a ministry's list and an epidemic — and neither is a commercial decision.

properties.name: Tianjin Ringpu Bio-Technology
properties.desc: A major Chinese veterinary biologics manufacturer producing poultry and other livestock vaccines, investing in bioreactor capacity and quality systems with the stated ambition of competing internationally. It belongs on this map beside the European and American vectored-vaccine producers for one reason: poultry is where recombinant vector vaccines are used most heavily anywhere, China raises more poultry than any other country, and until this round the facet recorded only Western manufacturers. A picture of who administers engineered viruses to birds that omits the largest poultry sector on Earth is not a picture of the industry.

properties.name: Stichting Taurus
properties.state: Netherlands — with breeding herds in six countries
properties.desc: The Dutch foundation that started the Tauros Programme in 2008 and runs its breeding, with scientific support from Wageningen University. The aurochs was hunted to extinction in 1627 but its genetics survive dispersed among older cattle breeds, and the programme crosses the closest of those breeds toward an animal that can graze European landscapes without supplementary feeding and alongside predators. A 2016 genetic study ranked 34 primitive breeds by closeness to a 6,700-year-old sequenced aurochs genome, which is how the parent stock is chosen. This is the entry that puts the rest of the facet in proportion: it pursues the same goal as the venture-funded de-extinction companies — an extinct animal's ecological function restored — using crossbreeding, published genomics and two decades, with no editing, no cloning, and no surrogate mothers.

properties.name: Rewilding Europe
properties.desc: The organisation that provides the land. Its 2015 partnership with the Dutch breeding foundation splits the work explicitly: the foundation runs the breeding, and this body supplies breeding locations across its rewilding areas and network. Herds now graze in Spain, Portugal, Croatia, Czechia, Romania and the Netherlands, with breeds chosen per site for local climate, forage and predators, and a stated goal of self-sufficient herds of at least 150 animals within about twenty years. Every other release on this map is a permit question — who authorised it, under which statute. This one is a land question: whoever holds the ground decides, and the animal is legally cattle.

properties.name: SweTree Technologies
properties.desc: A forest biotechnology company founded in 1999, owned by the forestry industry it serves — its main shareholders include three of Sweden's largest forest companies alongside a research holding vehicle. It holds first right of refusal on innovations from a company assembling around forty senior Swedish researchers, and works with the Umeå Plant Science Centre. Its core work is not transgenes: it is somatic embryogenesis, in which one seed is made to yield many embryos, so an elite tree can be copied at industrial scale. A pilot plant producing about 100,000 spruce seedlings a year is intended to become a factory at 20 million, co-owned by the same forest companies. That is clonal forestry rather than genetic engineering, and it raises the question this facet keeps circling: twenty million copies of a selected genotype is a narrowing of a forest's genetic base whether or not a single gene was inserted.

properties.name: Camcore
properties.desc: A non-profit international tree breeding cooperative formed in 1980 by private industry and hosted at a public university, with 27 members across 11 countries in the Americas, Africa and Asia, working on pines, eucalypts, gmelina and teak. What distinguishes it from other tree improvement programmes is stated on its own front page: alongside breeding, a major emphasis on establishing EX SITU CONSERVATION PLANTINGS of species and populations, including several threatened species native to the southern United States. A breeding cooperative that also plants living archives of the populations it draws from is doing something the biobanks elsewhere in this facet do in freezers — and the trees keep evolving.

properties.name: UPL Limited
properties.state: Mumbai — operations in more than 130 countries
properties.desc: Founded in 1969 making red phosphorus for matches, now by its own account the fifth largest agrochemical group in the world, with revenue above five billion dollars, more than 13,600 product registrations, and an integrated portfolio running from seeds through crop protection to post-harvest. It bought Advanta Seeds in 2015 and Arysta LifeScience in 2019. The map's seed facet is built around four majors that sell traits with matching herbicides; this is a fifth company of comparable reach assembled from the other direction, by an Indian chemicals manufacturer buying its way into seed. A generic agrochemical maker acquiring a global seed business ends up in the same position as the trait owners — selling the seed and the spray together — without ever having developed a transgene.

properties.name: Advanta Seeds — igrowth
properties.state: Hyderabad — one biotech centre and 20+ research stations
properties.desc: The seed arm's herbicide tolerance technology, which the company states plainly is proprietary and non-GMO: it lets a farmer spray an imidazolinone herbicide over the crop for broadleaf and grass control without damaging it. That combination — the commercial function of a herbicide-tolerant trait, reached without genetic modification and therefore outside every biosafety register on this map — is the reason it needs an entry of its own. A reader tracking herbicide-tolerant crops through approval databases will not find it, and the field it is sprayed on looks the same either way. The company reports more than 60 crops and a pipeline above 850 varieties across those stations.

properties.name: Medgene
properties.desc: A company built around a regulatory category rather than a product. In 2018 the US Department of Agriculture created a pathway allowing a vaccine PLATFORM to be licensed rather than each vaccine made on it, and Medgene's business is that pathway: it holds licences for prescription platform vaccines in cattle — influenza D, coronavirus, rotavirus, papillomavirus — and has produced them for swine, rabbits and deer, with a veterinarian required to prescribe and supervise each use. Because the platform was already approved in cattle it could move quickly on an H5N1 vaccine for dairy herds during the fourth year of the outbreak, reaching final review for conditional licence and a distribution agreement with one of the largest animal health companies. This is the most consequential regulatory idea in the facet: approve the method once and the organisms made on it need only a shorter review, which is what makes a rapid response possible and what makes the register of approved products stop describing what is actually in use.

properties.name: USDA Center for Veterinary Biologics
properties.desc: The US regulator for veterinary vaccines, and the body that created the prescription platform category in 2018. Its handling of the dairy cattle H5N1 question shows what such a regulator actually weighs: the virus is classified highly pathogenic, so testing required a containment level demanding three barriers and showering in and out, until a 2024 notice allowed studies outside containment facilities and shortened the path. Against that sat a trade consideration named openly by the developers — international agreements could penalise dairy products from vaccinated animals. A vaccine decision here is simultaneously a biosafety judgement, a laboratory-capacity question and an export negotiation, and the last of those is rarely visible in any register.

properties.name: Vivotecnia
properties.desc: A Spanish contract research organisation operating since 2000, running toxicology and safety studies on monkeys, dogs, pigs, rabbits, rats and mice for the pharmaceutical, chemical, cosmetic, tobacco and food industries. In April 2021 an animal technician who had worked there between 2018 and 2020 released undercover footage through a campaign organisation; after an inspection the Madrid regional government said it had confirmed signs of mistreatment and suspended activity, and police animal protection services were contacted. The company's chief executive said he was shocked by the images. What happened next is the reason for the entry rather than the footage. The campaigners later reported that the suspension had covered only NEW projects while experiments already under way continued, that the animals were not rehomed as expected, and that testing was subsequently permitted to resume while legal action continued. The facility has held public research funding. A suspension that stops new work and leaves existing work running is a different instrument from the one the announcement describes, and this map should record which kind a regulator actually used.

properties.name: Comunidad de Madrid — animal facility licensing
properties.desc: The regional authority that issues licences to animal testing facilities in the Madrid region and inspects them. It ordered an inspection within a day of the 2021 footage being published, confirmed signs of mistreatment, and announced a suspension — then, according to the organisations pursuing the case, did not respond to requests for information about the animals still held at the site, and later allowed testing to resume. It appears on this map because sub-national regulators almost never do, and because the licensing power over a laboratory sits at that level in Spain rather than nationally. Whoever grants the licence is who a complaint has to reach, and in this instance that was a regional environment department rather than a research or health ministry.

properties.name: Genetic Savings & Clone
properties.desc: The first commercial pet cloning company, opened in 2000 with more than ten million dollars from a single backer, and closed at the end of 2006 having told clients it could not develop the technology to the point where cloning pets was commercially viable. Its record is precise and instructive: it funded the first cloned cat, produced five cloned cats in all, and sold two, the first for a reported $50,000 before the price was cut to $32,000. It never cloned a dog, which was the founder's original purpose. Alongside the cloning it ran a tissue bank, charging several hundred clients an annual fee to store material against a future clone — a service sold years before the service it was for could be delivered. The pet tissue banks operating today are the same proposition, and this is the case where the second half never arrived and the fees were refunded.

properties.name: BioArts International
properties.desc: The successor venture, run by the same chief executive, which in 2008 auctioned five dog cloning slots online with bids opening at $100,000. The cloning itself was to be carried out by the South Korean laboratory whose founder's human stem cell work had been found fraudulent — a laboratory that is separately on this map for having gone on to clone hundreds of dogs. The reasoning given for trying again is worth recording: the earlier company's tissue banking business had shown there was demand, even though its cloning business had failed, and dog owners were held to differ from cat owners. That is a market read taken from a storage product and applied to a service, and it is the same read the surviving pet cloning and tissue banking companies are still working from.

properties.name: The Quagga Project
properties.state: Elandsberg Farms, Western Cape, South Africa
properties.desc: Begun in 1987 by a museum taxidermist who had remounted a quagga foal in 1969 and kept tissue from it, which later allowed the DNA work showing the quagga was not a separate species but a subspecies of the plains zebra. On that basis the project selectively bred southern plains zebras for reduced striping and a browner body, drawing founder stock from as far as Zululand and Namibia. Within four generations animals were born whose coat pattern closely resembles museum specimens. The regulatory outcome is the part that could not have been predicted: the agriculture minister declared the rebred animal, named the Rau quagga after the project's founder, a landrace breed under the Animal Improvement Act. A recovered wild phenotype was recognised by the state not as a restored subspecies but as a breed of livestock, which is the same legal category the back-bred European cattle occupy — arrived at independently on another continent.

properties.name: Grazelands Rewilding
properties.desc: The organisation now named alongside the European rewilding body as running the aurochs back-breeding work in practice — the day-to-day herd management across the breeding sites, distinct from both the foundation that started the programme and the network that supplies the land. It is worth recording separately because this facet's venture-funded companies are single corporations doing everything, while the back-breeding side is three or four bodies each holding one function: the science, the herds, the ground, and the genetics. Whether that division is a weakness or the reason the programme has run for nearly two decades is a question a reader can now put to both models from the same map.

properties.name: Ceva Phylaxia
properties.state: Budapest — with a second plant at Monor
properties.desc: The largest single research and production site in its parent's global vaccine network, on a Budapest campus that began in 1912 as the Phylaxia Serum Producing Company and made the first vaccine against classical swine fever. Over 95 per cent of its output is exported. The historical thread is the entry: the herpesvirus vector used in poultry hatchery vaccines worldwide carries the name of a veterinary scientist who worked at this site, and the diseases named after him and a colleague are still the ones being vaccinated against, in billions of doses a year, using a virus named for the man who described the disease. A second plant at Monor is being built for fermentation-based inactivated vaccines at more than eight billion doses annually. The parent describes itself as the historical world leader in vector vaccines for poultry and states it has built an mRNA platform for animals.

properties.name: Vaksindo
properties.state: Indonesia — part of the Japfa Comfeed group
properties.desc: The first animal vaccine manufacturer in Indonesia, producing livestock vaccines mainly for poultry used in hatcheries, breeding farms and commercial farms — and, by its own description, a strategic link in the value chain of the feed and protein group that owns it. That ownership is the point. Elsewhere in this facet a vaccine maker sells to farms it does not own; here the manufacturer, the feed supplier and the farming operation are one group, in the country with one of the largest poultry sectors in Southeast Asia. Vertical integration decides what gets vaccinated against and when, without any purchase decision being made at the farm at all.

properties.name: International Institute of Tropical Agriculture (IITA)
properties.state: Ibadan, Nigeria — with research stations across Africa
properties.desc: A non-profit research institute founded in 1967 by the Ford and Rockefeller foundations, now part of the CGIAR system, headquartered in Ibadan with stations across Africa. Its cowpea breeding programme has released improved varieties in seventy countries, and it maintains the multi-location trial networks against which those varieties are judged. It matters to this facet because the Bt cowpea that Nigeria approved in 2019 — the first engineered food crop cleared for commercial release anywhere in Africa — and its Ghanaian counterpart sit inside that programme's crop and its trial system. Confined field trials of a second-generation construct have run in Nigeria, Ghana and Burkina Faso. The trial plots behind Africa's engineered food crop are held by a philanthropically founded international institute, not by a company and not by a national government.

properties.name: AGROSAVIA
properties.state: Mosquera, Cundinamarca — Colombian agricultural research corporation
properties.desc: Colombia's national agricultural research corporation, successor to the institute that built the country's national germplasm bank in the 1960s under a Rockefeller Foundation collaboration. It breeds and releases cultivars under its own name across crops and forages, runs the trial network they are tested in, and works jointly with Argentina's federal institute on the maize and soybean system. Its presence completes a pattern this map has now recorded four times over: in Argentina, Brazil, Nigeria and Colombia the plots where varieties are tested belong to state or international institutes, while in Europe and North America the same work is bought from private contractors. Which of those a country has determines whether trial data is a public record or a commercial confidence.

properties.name: CTNBio — engineered eucalyptus approvals
properties.state: Brasília — Comissão Técnica Nacional de Biossegurança
properties.desc: Brazil is the only country to have released engineered trees for commercial-scale cultivation, and this commission is where every one of those decisions was taken. Event H421, which overexpresses an Arabidopsis gene to increase wood volume, was developed in 2000, field-tested under regulation from 2006 to 2015 across three states, and approved in 2015 as the first genetically modified eucalyptus approved anywhere. Nine approvals have followed: five herbicide-tolerant events since 2021, an insect-resistant Bt event in 2023, a double stack later that year and a triple stack in March 2024, the first anywhere. Post-release monitoring ran five consecutive years with annual reports. Eucalyptus covers roughly 7.5 million hectares in Brazil. Set this against New Zealand felling its trial trees at eight years and China unable to say how much poplar was planted: three regulators, three entirely different answers to the same organism.

properties.name: Nippon Paper Industries
properties.desc: One of the Japanese paper manufacturers that pursued engineered eucalyptus for pulping rather than for yield or pest resistance: its research aimed at blocking genes controlling stages of lignin synthesis, producing trees with less lignin and more cellulose. Competitors pursued the same end by different routes, one targeting lower lignin content directly and another making lignin easier to remove during processing so that less bleaching agent is needed. The distinction is worth holding: the crop side of this map is dominated by traits that change what happens in the FIELD, and this is a trait designed to change what happens in the MILL. A tree engineered to be easier to dissolve is a different proposition from one engineered to resist an insect, and the plantations these companies hold sit in Papua New Guinea, New Zealand, Australia and Viet Nam rather than in Japan.

properties.name: Corte Constitucional de Colombia — Sentencia T-968 de 2009
properties.desc: The 2009 judgment that is the entire legal basis for surrogacy in Colombia. It held that nothing in Colombian law expressly prohibits such agreements, and set out conditions for them — but it did not create a framework for the contract, for parentage, or for the medical and financial obligations owed to the surrogate. One summary puts it exactly: the court authorised surrogacy without regulating it. More than sixteen bills to legislate have been introduced over roughly two decades and none has passed, so the practice runs on judicial tolerance, with the court issuing further rulings since. In practice the surrogate may appear on the birth certificate and parentage is established after birth through court proceedings, which vary by judge. This is the third distinct legal condition this facet now records: a country that regulates surrogacy, a country that prohibits it, and a country where it exists because nothing forbids it.

properties.name: Korea Institute of Toxicology (KIT)
properties.state: Daejeon — Daedeok Science Town, with a Jeonbuk branch
properties.desc: A government-funded institute under South Korea's science ministry that assesses the safety of medicines, pesticides, food additives, cosmetics and industrial chemicals, and sells non-clinical assessment as a service. Its good laboratory practice system is certified against both OECD and US food and drug administration criteria, and it was the first organisation in Asia accredited by the international laboratory animal care body. Its predictive toxicology department works on in vitro and in silico methods intended to replace animal tests. Two things make it the right entry for this facet's last hole: a state institute competing as a contract laboratory is a different actor from the listed companies that dominate here, and a body whose income depends on animal studies is simultaneously developing the methods meant to displace them.

properties.name: Biotoxtech
properties.state: Ochang, Cheongju, North Chungcheong — with subsidiaries
properties.desc: A Korean contract research organisation running non-clinical safety studies for pharmaceuticals, food, cosmetics, cell therapies, chemicals and agrochemicals from a facility of around 146,000 square feet, and it states it is the only domestic private CRO to hold good laboratory practice accreditation from the US food and drug administration, alongside full international laboratory animal care accreditation. Its group divides the work across subsidiaries: one for non-clinical pharmacology and bioanalysis including PCR-based biodistribution for cell and gene therapies, and another offering primate-based toxicology and efficacy studies and inhalation toxicology. Biodistribution studies for gene therapies are how a regulator learns where an engineered vector travels in a body, and that work sits here.

properties.name: Leibniz Institute DSMZ
properties.desc: The German national collection of microorganisms and cell cultures, and the European counterpart to the American reference collection: it authenticates and holds strains for the long term rather than circulating engineered constructs. Its position in Europe also puts it inside the access and benefit-sharing rules that govern where a strain came from and who is owed what for it — a question the crop side of this map asks constantly about germplasm and the microbial side rarely asks at all.

properties.name: US Fish and Wildlife Service — Office of Law Enforcement
properties.desc: The agency that clears or refuses live-animal imports at the US border, and the reason the laboratory primate trade changed shape after 2022. Following the indictment of a Cambodian supplier's officers, it declined to clear Cambodian shipments without incontrovertible evidence that the animals were purpose-bred. The largest US contract research organisation, which had sourced around 60 per cent of its primates from Cambodia, suspended imports and warned investors of a two to four hundred basis point hit to revenue growth; a competitor that had taken $140 million from Cambodian monkeys in 2022 lost most of its market value in a week. The industry has since been working on genetic testing to prove captive breeding — which is an admission that the paperwork never could.

properties.name: Bolsa de Comercio de Rosario
properties.desc: Argentina's principal grain exchange, and one of the bodies that opposed the engineered wheat approval alongside the provincial exchanges, the Chamber of Industrial Milling and the farm organisations of the liaison table. The objection was not about eating it. It was that once the engineered variety moves through the same elevators, trucks and ships as the conventional crop, keeping the two apart stops being possible and the value of the conventional crop in export markets goes with it. An exchange exists to price and move grain, so when one argues against a new variety it is arguing about the handling system rather than the biology.

properties.name: FastBio
properties.state: Ribeirão Preto, São Paulo — Supera Parque de Inovação e Tecnologia
properties.desc: Founded in 2011 by a group of PhDs and based in a science park at Ribeirão Preto, selling gene synthesis, oligonucleotides, peptides, proteins, antibodies and a CRISPR platform to Brazilian universities, technology firms and industry. It describes itself as a leader in the DISTRIBUTION of biotechnology products and services, and its own gene synthesis page names GenScript as the partner whose technology performs the work. That is the entry. Brazil's DNA synthesis market was around $62 million in 2023, the largest in Latin America and about two per cent of the world's, and the comprehensive lists of firms that manufacture synthetic DNA contain no South American entry at all. Screening works because an order has to pass through a provider who reads the sequence and checks the customer; where the order is placed in Brazil and filled abroad, that check is made in the jurisdiction that manufactures rather than the one that will host whatever is built. A customer testimonial on the company's own front page describes a gene import that was very slow because of the funding agency's procedure, which is the same distance measured in weeks.

properties.name: Ecocert
properties.desc: Certification is the mechanism by which a crop is declared free of engineered material, and this map holds 144 rows naming who certifies without naming the largest of them. Ecocert began as a control body spun out of a French organic advisers' association in 1991, and now operates through some 27 to 30 subsidiaries in more than 130 countries; it reports inspecting around 70% of the French organic sector and about 30% worldwide. It grew partly by acquisition — the Institute for Marketecology in 2013, IMOgroup in 2014, and a US certifier in 2019 — and is controlled by the family holding company of its co-founder. Two things follow. A grower in most countries deals with a local subsidiary of a multinational rather than a body founded where they farm. And the EU stopped accepting organic certification on raw Indian cotton from several major certifiers including this one, after fraudulent certificates — the check on the supply chain failing in the same way the supply chain does.

properties.name: Control Union Certifications
properties.desc: A for-profit certification division of a Dutch inspection group founded in 1920, operating in 70 to 80 countries. It was established in 2002 as a joint venture with Skal, the Dutch foundation that supervises the organic market — so a commercial certifier was set up in partnership with the body that oversees organic operators, which is a different arrangement from a certifier merely being accredited by one. Its parent runs laboratory analysis, pest management, collateral management and vessel performance services alongside the certification arm, for agriculture, energy, maritime and textiles: the same group inspects a cargo, tests it, and certifies the standard it is sold under. Named alongside Ecocert among the certifiers whose organic certification of raw Indian cotton the EU stopped accepting after fraudulent certificates.

properties.name: Food certification market — the testing, inspection and certification firms
properties.desc: The bodies that certify food are largely the same firms that certify everything else. Market surveys of food certification name DEKRA, SGS, Intertek, AsureQuality, Bureau Veritas, LRQA, DNV, TÜV SÜD, Kiwa, ALS, UL, Assurecloud and Control Union — general testing, inspection and certification groups, several of them publicly listed, for whom organic and non-GM claims are one product line among many. The stated growth strategies are geographical expansion into emerging economies and acquisition to gain a foothold across the supply chain. This map's per-country resources name national certifiers almost exclusively; in most countries the certificate a grower holds is issued by a local subsidiary of one of these.

properties.name: Bureau Veritas
properties.desc: Founded 1828, listed in Paris, present in about 140 countries with roughly 82,000 employees and 2025 revenue of €6.47bn; its largest shareholder is the investment company Wendel with about 35.5%. It appears on every published list of the firms that test food and feed for engineered content, and on the lists of the firms that certify organic and non-GM claims. It bought a Chinese food testing company in 2019, and China had already become its largest market by revenue and staff two years earlier. A grower's certificate, a shipment's test and an importing country's compliance check are, in this sector, products sold by listed companies with growth targets — which is a different arrangement from a state inspectorate, whatever the standard being applied.

properties.name: Kiwa
properties.desc: Founded 1948, private, owned by the Dutch industrial holding company SHV, with 2023 revenue around €1.3bn and about 11,000 staff in more than 35 countries. Its organic arm certifies to the EU organic regulation, the US National Organic Program, the private Bio Suisse standard, the Naturland association's standard and a supermarket's own protocol, among others. That is the mechanism worth recording: a single commercial certifier holds the keys to a public regulation, a foreign government's programme, a farming association's private standard and a retailer's contractual requirement at the same time, and a producer meets all four through one auditor. Its growth since 2000 has been by acquisition — Gastec, Inspecta and Vinçotte among them.

properties.name: AsureQuality
properties.desc: A New Zealand government-owned company selling food assurance commercially: laboratories, auditing, organic certification, and the country's recognised meat inspection agency. It is a recognised agency for the Ministry for Primary Industries to provide third-party assurance where government-to-government official assurance is required — so a state function is discharged by a company the state owns and which competes for the same work commercially. It markets its government ownership as a selling point for its organic mark. In the same domestic market BioGro certifies for export and domestic sale, and OrganicFarmNZ offers lower-cost certification for smaller producers selling only domestically: three tiers, one of them owned by the regulator's own shareholder.

properties.name: TÜV, DEKRA, DNV, LRQA and the rest of the certification field
properties.desc: Beyond the firms with their own entries here, published surveys of food certification name DEKRA SE, DNV, ALS Limited, TÜV SÜD, Lloyd's Register, Kiwa, NSF International, Socotec, Aspirata in South Africa, and Indocert, TQ Cert and MS Certification Services in India. The TÜV organisations show the scale involved: TÜV Nord alone, founded 1869, employs more than 15,000 people in over 100 countries. Their certification lines cover food safety, organic, quality management, gluten-free, halal, kosher, non-GMO, fair trade and sustainability — non-GMO certification is one product in a catalogue sold to manufacturers, retailers, restaurants, caterers and agricultural producers. The per-country resources on this map name national certifiers; this is the field they sit in.

properties.name: Skal Biocontrole
properties.desc: The body the Dutch state charges with supervising the organic market: it registers operators, inspects them and issues the certification without which nothing may be sold as organic in the Netherlands. It is also the foundation that entered the 2002 joint venture which became Control Union Certifications, the commercial certifier now working in 70 to 80 countries. The supervisor of one national organic market helped found a global certification business, and both appear on this map: one as a regulator, one as a company whose organic certification of raw Indian cotton the EU stopped accepting.

properties.name: IOAS — accreditation of organic certifiers
properties.desc: Accredits organic certification bodies worldwide and publishes which ones it accredits. This is the layer above the certifiers on this map: a certifier's own site will always say it is accredited, and only an accreditor's register says whether that is still true. It is not the only such list — the EU publishes recognised control bodies for organic imports, each with a code of the form XX-BIO-NNN printed on the product label, and the US and others run their own — so a body may be on one list and not another. Recognition has been withdrawn: the EU stopped accepting several major certifiers' organic certification of raw Indian cotton after fraudulent certificates.

properties.name: TEVAH Consulting
properties.desc: The regulatory-consulting facet of this map holds fourteen records, twelve of them in North America and Europe, which reads as though dossier work is done only where the biggest regulators sit. Brazil approves more engineered organisms than almost anywhere, and this is one of the firms that prepares the submissions. Its listed services describe the whole apparatus a Brazilian applicant must satisfy: biosafety manuals, training for the in-house biosafety commission each institution must maintain, the annual biosafety inspections CTNBio requires, commercial dossiers and their submission, following the file in Brasília, answering requests for further information, and registration with the agriculture ministry, the environment institute and the health agency as applicable. It also develops PCR and ELISA detection kits — the same firm that writes the dossier can supply the test for what it describes. Its consultants are described as drawn from academic institutions and the agricultural biotechnology industry.

properties.name: Genetic Technology (Precision Breeding) Act — in force in England
properties.desc: Sixty-six UK records sit on this map and none of them recorded the change that matters most: the Act passed in March 2023 came into force on 13 November 2025, its secondary legislation finalised the previous May. It removes plants and animals produced by modern biotechnology, and food and feed derived from them, from GMO regulation where the organism could have occurred naturally or been produced by traditional methods. In their place, two tiers: a marketing notice from Defra, then a food and feed authorisation from the Food Standards Agency, Tier 1 a lighter assessment and Tier 2 a bespoke one. The regulations require the FSA to keep a public food and feed register naming each authorised organism, its reference number, the authorisation-holder, the purpose of the intended genetic change and a safety summary. Two limits: it applies to ENGLAND ONLY, the Scottish and Welsh Parliaments having withheld legislative consent, and the secondary legislation for ANIMALS has not been laid. Commentary describing the reform places England alongside Canada, Australia, Brazil, Argentina, the United States and Japan.

properties.name: Gene Technology Amendment Regulations 2019 and FSANZ P1055 — Australia's carve-out
properties.desc: The map holds nineteen Australian records, including two on the Gene Technology Regulator praising it as one of the few regulators that publishes field trial coordinates before a decision. None recorded what that regulator no longer sees. Amendments to the Gene Technology Regulations 2001, notified 4 April 2019 and in effect from October, revised the schedule of organisms that are not GMOs: an SDN-1 edit, where a site-directed nuclease is used with NO REPAIR TEMPLATE and no foreign DNA remains, is outside the definition. SDN-2, which uses an artificially created template, stays inside it. The food side followed separately: FSANZ Proposal P1055, opened February 2020 with two public consultations and 1,736 submissions on the first, replaced the process-based definition with a new definition of genetically modified food including a list of exemptions and a definition of null segregant. FSANZ's own account names the alignment: Canada, Japan and England. So the regulator whose transparency this map holds up as a standard publishes trial locations for the organisms still inside the definition, and nothing for those outside it.

properties.name: Gene Technology Bill — ending New Zealand's outdoor ban
properties.desc: Recorded here as a bill rather than a law, which is the accurate state of it. It would end a nearly thirty-year restriction on genetically modified organisms outside the laboratory, moving gene technology out of the Hazardous Substances and New Organisms Act 1996 into a standalone risk-tiered regime, and creating a Gene Technology Regulator: a statutory officer appointed by the minister, employed and supported by the Environmental Protection Authority, accountable to the EPA for employment and to the minister otherwise. The regulator could exempt technologies assessed as minimal risk or indistinguishable from conventional breeding. The government stated the model is closely based on Australia's Gene Technology Act 2000. The scale of the response is worth recording: the Health Committee received 14,458 written submissions and heard 287 oral submitters, reporting back on 10 October 2025. Objections on the record include the absence of any coexistence provision for conventional and organic growers, left to industry to resolve, and a confidentiality carry-over from HSNO that the Chief Ombudsman noted risks protecting information that ought to be released.

properties.name: Office Memorandum of 30 March 2022 — India's SDN-1 and SDN-2 exemption
properties.state: New Delhi — MoEFCC, Indira Paryavaran Bhawan
properties.desc: Forty Indian records sit on this map — GEAC, the Department of Biotechnology, the seed industry, the Bt cotton and Bt brinjal history, the litigation — and none of them recorded the exemption. The Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change issued an Office Memorandum on 30 March 2022 exempting genome-edited plants in the SDN-1 and SDN-2 categories, free of exogenous introduced DNA, from Rules 7 to 11 of the 1989 Rules made under the Environment (Protection) Act 1986. Those rules cover import and export, manufacture and processing, environmental release and food use — so the exemption removes the approval requirement rather than adjusting it. The Department of Biotechnology issued risk assessment guidelines in May 2022, and standard operating procedures for regulatory review were notified on 4 October 2022, placing the residual oversight with Institutional Biosafety Committees inside the organisations doing the work. India's exemption goes further than Australia's, which covers SDN-1 only and leaves SDN-2 regulated. A published policy brief also urged that foods from SDN-1 and SDN-2 should not be treated as genetically engineered under the Food Safety and Standards Act 2006.

properties.name: JDC No. 1 s.2021 and DA Memorandum Circular No. 8 s.2022 — the Philippine route
properties.desc: The Philippine carve-out works differently from the exemptions elsewhere on this map, and the difference is worth having. Rather than declaring a class of edits outside the rules, the 2021 Joint Department Circular of five departments — science, agriculture, environment, health and interior — states that products of new breeding innovations which do not contain novel combinations of genetic material obtained through modern biotechnology are not covered by it, and DA Memorandum Circular No. 8 of May 2022 sets out how each product is EVALUATED to determine which side of that line it falls. So there is a case-by-case determination and a body making it, where India and Australia wrote a category-wide exemption. The same 2021 revision cut the public comment period from 60 days to 15 working days, in the name of an ease of doing business act; applications and biosafety permits for commercial propagation and direct use are still required to be posted publicly on the NCBP and Bureau of Plant Industry websites.

properties.name: Genome editing guidelines — Ghana, Nigeria, Kenya and Malawi
properties.desc: Ghana's National Biosafety Authority published Guidelines on Genome Editing on 30 October 2023, setting out which categories of genome-edited organisms and products are regulated under the Biosafety Act 2011 (Act 831) — making it the fourth African country with validated genome-editing guidelines, after Nigeria, Kenya and Malawi. Four of the countries whose biosafety authorities this map already records have therefore drawn the same line as Argentina, and none of those records mentioned it. Note what the instrument is in each case: guidelines issued by the biosafety authority under an existing biosafety act, rather than an exemption from it — the regulator keeps the decision about what falls inside its own statute.
